---
title: "The Game in Fifteen Minutes"
subtitle: "Field, scoring and clock: the lines on the grass, the five ways to score, and the two clocks that decide what a team can afford to do."
description: "Every marking on an NFL field and what it is for, why the hash marks create a wide side and a short side (and why college looks so different), every way to score and why the gap between seven points and three drives so many decisions, when the game clock runs and stops, the 40-second play clock, and the shape of a game from coin toss to overtime."
glossary:
  "End zone": "The 10-yard-deep area at each end of the field, between the goal line and the end line. Carry the ball into it, or catch or recover it there, and you score a touchdown."
  "Goal line": "The line that separates the field of play from the end zone. It belongs to the end zone: a ball on, above or past it, held by a runner, is a touchdown."
  "Yard line": "Any line across the field parallel to the goal lines, named by its distance from the nearer goal line ('the 35'). Lines are painted every 5 yards, with a short tick at every yard."
  "Hash marks": "The two rows of short lines running the length of the field, 70 feet 9 inches in from each sideline in the NFL. Every play starts on or between them; if the last play ended outside them, the ball goes on the nearer one."
  "Field side": {def: "When the ball is on a hash, the side of the field with more room between the ball and the sideline.", aliases: ["Wide side"]}
  "Boundary side": {def: "When the ball is on a hash, the side nearer the sideline, with less room.", aliases: ["Short side"]}
  "Sideline": "One of the two long boundary lines along the sides of the field. The sideline itself is out of bounds."
  "Touchdown": "Six points, scored by carrying the ball into the opponent's end zone, or by catching or recovering it there."
  "Extra point": {def: "The one-point kick after a touchdown. In the NFL it has been snapped from the 15-yard line since 2015, which makes it a 33-yard kick.", aliases: ["PAT"]}
  "Two-point conversion": "The alternative to the extra point: one play from the 2-yard line, worth two points if the ball is run or caught into the end zone."
  "Field goal": "Three points for kicking the ball, held on the ground by a holder, through the goal posts on a play from scrimmage. It can be tried from anywhere, on any down; a miss gives the other team the ball at the spot of the kick (or at its own 20, if the kick was from inside it)."
  "Safety (score)": "Two points for the defense when the offense's ball carrier is downed in his own end zone (or the offense fouls there). The team scored on must then kick the ball away from its own 20."
  "Possession": "Control of the ball. The team that has it is the offense; one unbroken stretch of having the ball is also called a possession."
  "Quarter": "One of the four 15-minute periods of game-clock time in an NFL game. Teams switch ends after the first and third."
  "Two-minute warning": "An automatic timeout in the second and fourth quarters, taken after the last play that started with more than 2:00 on the game clock."
  "Timeout": "A stoppage a team calls to stop the clock (and to talk). Each team gets three per half, and two in a regular-season overtime."
  "Game clock": "The scoreboard clock that counts down each 15-minute quarter. It runs during plays and, depending on how the last play ended, between them."
  "Play clock": "The countdown between plays: 40 seconds from the end of the last play, or 25 after certain stoppages. The offense must snap the ball before it reaches zero."

```{python}
#| code-summary: "Show the Python (shared drawing helpers for this chapter)"
import os
import logging
import textwrap

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.patches import FancyBboxPatch, FancyArrowPatch, Rectangle, Ellipse, Polygon

import gridiron.field as gfield
from gridiron import Field, Play, Player, offense, defense, routes as r, style, draw_marker
from gridiron import FIELD_WIDTH, HASH_NEAR, HASH_FAR

logging.getLogger("matplotlib.font_manager").setLevel(logging.ERROR)
style.apply()

MID = FIELD_WIDTH / 2
GOLD = "#d9a21b"           # goal posts
PYLON = "#f07d1a"          # pylons
BORDER = "#d9d8d0"         # the 6-foot white border, drawn light gray so it shows on a white page
FIELD_TINT = "#dcebf7"     # field (wide) side
BOUNDARY_TINT = "#f6e3c9"  # boundary (short) side


def blank(ax):
    ax.set_axis_off()
    ax.grid(False)


def box(ax, x, y, w, h, text, fc=style.SURFACE, ec=style.BASELINE, lw=1.0, fs=8.5,
        bold=False, color=style.INK, sub=None, sub_fs=7):
    """A rounded box centred on (x, y) in data units, with an optional smaller subtitle."""
    ax.add_patch(FancyBboxPatch((x - w / 2, y - h / 2), w, h, boxstyle="round,pad=0.02,rounding_size=1.2",
                                fc=fc, ec=ec, lw=lw, zorder=3))
    if sub:
        ax.text(x, y + h * 0.18, text, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=fs, color=color,
                fontweight="bold" if bold else "normal", zorder=4)
        ax.text(x, y - h * 0.2, sub, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=sub_fs, color=style.INK_2,
                zorder=4, linespacing=1.15)
    else:
        ax.text(x, y, text, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=fs, color=color,
                fontweight="bold" if bold else "normal", zorder=4, linespacing=1.2)


def arrow(ax, p0, p1, color=style.INK_2, lw=1.2, ls="-", rad=0.0, head=10, z=5):
    ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch(p0, p1, arrowstyle="-|>", mutation_scale=head, color=color, lw=lw,
                                 ls=ls, shrinkA=1, shrinkB=1, connectionstyle=f"arc3,rad={rad}", zorder=z))


def callout(ax, text, xy, xytext, fs=7, ha="center"):
    """A label off the drawing with a thin leader line to the thing it names."""
    ax.annotate(text, xy=xy, xytext=xytext, fontsize=fs, ha=ha, va="center", color=style.INK, zorder=9,
                linespacing=1.15,
                arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-", color=style.INK_2, lw=0.7, shrinkA=1, shrinkB=1.5),
                bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.2", fc=style.SURFACE, ec="none"))


def football(ax, x, y, w=2.4, h=1.4, angle=0, z=12):
    ax.add_patch(Ellipse((x, y), w, h, angle=angle, facecolor=style.BALL, edgecolor="white", lw=0.8, zorder=z))


def field_extras(fld, posts=True, pylons=True, try_lines=True, border=True, pylon_size=1.1):
    """What gridiron's Field doesn't draw: the white border, goal posts, pylons and the 2-yard
    try marks. Works in either orientation through fld.xy()."""
    ax, P = fld.ax, fld.xy
    if border:
        (x0, y0), (x1, y1) = P(-2.0, -2.0), P(122.0, FIELD_WIDTH + 2.0)
        lo_x, hi_x = sorted([float(x0), float(x1)])
        lo_y, hi_y = sorted([float(y0), float(y1)])
        ax.add_patch(Rectangle((lo_x, lo_y), hi_x - lo_x, hi_y - lo_y, facecolor=BORDER, edgecolor="none",
                               zorder=-1))
    if try_lines:
        for x in (12.0, 108.0):
            if fld.x0 <= x <= fld.x1:
                px, py = P([x, x], [MID - 0.5, MID + 0.5])
                ax.plot(px, py, color=style.INK_2, lw=1.4, zorder=1.5, solid_capstyle="butt")
    if pylons:
        for x in (0.0, 10.0, 110.0, 120.0):
            if fld.x0 - 0.01 <= x <= fld.x1 + 0.01:
                for y in (0.0, FIELD_WIDTH):
                    px, py = P(x, y)
                    ax.add_patch(Rectangle((float(px) - pylon_size / 2, float(py) - pylon_size / 2), pylon_size,
                                           pylon_size, facecolor=PYLON, edgecolor="white", lw=0.4, zorder=6))
    if posts:
        half = 18.5 / 3 / 2   # uprights 18 ft 6 in apart
        for x, back in ((0.0, -1.0), (120.0, 1.0)):
            if fld.x0 - 0.01 <= x <= fld.x1 + 0.01:
                px, py = P([x, x], [MID - half, MID + half])
                ax.plot(px, py, color=GOLD, lw=3.0, zorder=6, solid_capstyle="round")
                sx, sy = P([x, x + back * 1.6], [MID, MID])  # single post, offset behind the end line
                ax.plot(sx, sy, color=GOLD, lw=2.0, zorder=6)


class hashes_at:
    """Temporarily draw gridiron Fields with non-NFL hash marks (college, high school).
    gridiron.field reads HASH_NEAR / HASH_FAR when it draws, so we swap them and put them back."""

    def __init__(self, from_sideline):
        self.near, self.far = from_sideline, FIELD_WIDTH - from_sideline

    def __enter__(self):
        self.saved = (gfield.HASH_NEAR, gfield.HASH_FAR)
        gfield.HASH_NEAR, gfield.HASH_FAR = self.near, self.far
        return self

    def __exit__(self, *exc):
        gfield.HASH_NEAR, gfield.HASH_FAR = self.saved
        return False


def clip_texts(ax):
    """Hide any field number or label that falls outside a cropped field window."""
    for t in ax.texts:
        t.set_clip_on(True)


def hide_numbers(ax):
    """Hide the painted yard numbers where they would sit under a formation or a note."""
    for t in ax.texts:
        if t.get_text().strip().isdigit():
            t.set_visible(False)


def ch1(players):
    """This chapter's marker letters. The linemen (center included) stay blank, so 'C' only ever
    means a cornerback here, and every running back is 'R' (never 'T', which is a defensive tackle)."""
    out = []
    for q in players:
        if q.side == "off" and q.key in ("LT", "LG", "C", "RG", "RT"):
            q = q.moved(label="")
        elif q.side == "off" and q.pos in ("RB", "TB"):
            q = q.moved(label="R")
        out.append(q)
    return out


def time_pass(p, key, catch_t):
    """Throw so the ball arrives when `key` is where he is at catch_t (the catch, not the run after it)."""
    from gridiron.play import BALL_SPEED
    target = np.asarray(p.position(key, catch_t))
    t = catch_t - 1.0
    for _ in range(6):
        t = catch_t - float(np.linalg.norm(target - np.asarray(p.ball_position(t)))) / BALL_SPEED
    p.pass_to(key, t=t)
```

```{python}
rz = drives[drives.red_zone == 1]
rz_td, rz_fg = (rz.result == "Touchdown").mean(), (rz.result == "Field goal").mean()

                                     "qb_kneel", "qb_spike"]).sum() / n_games
scrimmage_per_game = r25.play_type.isin(["run", "pass"]).sum() / n_games
safeties_25 = int(r25.safety.sum())

# the try after a touchdown
xp_rate = reg[reg.extra_point_result.notna()].groupby("season").extra_point_result.apply(lambda s: (s == "good").mean())
tp_rate = reg[reg.two_point_conv_result.notna()].groupby("season").two_point_conv_result.apply(lambda s: (s == "success").mean())

# field goals by distance, last five seasons

fg["bucket"] = pd.cut(fg.kick_distance, [0, 29, 39, 49, 59, 80],
                      labels=["under 30", "30–39", "40–49", "50–59", "60+"])

# fourth-and-goal from the 1 or 2, 2016-2025: how often a run or pass scores
g4 = reg[reg.season.between(2016, 2025) & (reg.down == 4) & (reg.goal_to_go == 1) & (reg.yardline_100 <= 2)]

# after a safety: where the scoring team's next snap is, 2016-2025 (yards from its own goal line)
r16 = reg[reg.season.between(2016, 2025)].reset_index(drop=True)
after_safety = []
for i in r16.index[r16.safety == 1]:
    nxt = r16.iloc[i + 1:i + 8]
    nxt = nxt[(nxt.game_id == r16.game_id[i]) & nxt.play_type.isin(["run", "pass"])]
    if len(nxt):
        after_safety.append(100 - nxt.yardline_100.iloc[0])
safety_start = float(np.median(after_safety))
```

Ninety seconds left in the first half. A receiver catches a pass over the middle, gets tackled,
and everyone sprints back to the line while the clock keeps ticking. One play later a
different receiver catches the *same* length of pass at the sideline and dives out of bounds,
and the broadcaster says "smart, he stopped the clock." A few drives after that, a team facing
fourth down a yard from the end zone sends out its kicker, and the home crowd boos the three
free points. Why does stepping on a white line save time? Why would anyone boo a sure
field goal? And why did the ball start on the left side of the field on one play and the
right side on the next? This chapter is the skeleton everything else in the book hangs on:
the field, the scoring and the clock.

Here is a fact to keep in mind as you read. An NFL broadcast lasts about three hours, the
game clock covers sixty minutes, and the ball is actually live for only about **11 minutes**.[^wsj]
Every play starts with a *snap*, the center handing the ball back between his legs (the full
anatomy of a play is in [What a Play Really Is](01-04-what-a-play-really-is.qmd)). Stitch every
snap-to-whistle together and a whole game fits inside one fifteen-minute quarter, with
time to spare. The other 49 minutes of game clock and two-plus hours of broadcast are what
the rest of this book is about: the decisions, the preparation and the waiting between
those few seconds of action. Most of what makes those decisions hard comes from the three
things in this chapter.

**You'll be able to…**

- Name every marking on an NFL field, say what it is for, and say which lines are in bounds
  and which are out.
- Find the field side and the boundary side on any snap, and explain why the hash the ball
  sits on changes what both teams do (and why college football looks so much wider).
- Score any play (touchdown, extra point, two-point try, field goal, safety) and explain why
  the gap between seven points and three drives so many coaching decisions.
- Say, after any play, whether the game clock is running and when it will start again.
- Tell the game clock from the play clock, and say what each one forces a team to do.
- Sketch the shape of a game: coin toss, kickoffs, possessions, quarters, the two-minute
  warning, halftime and overtime.

## The field: a 120-yard grid

An NFL field is a rectangle 120 yards long and 53⅓ yards (160 feet) wide.[^field] The odd width
is a fossil: the college rules convention of 1881 set the field at 110 by 53⅓ yards, and the
width has never changed since.[^width] It's easiest to learn as three pieces: a 100-yard **field of play** in the middle and a 10-yard
end zone at each end. Everything painted on it exists for one of three reasons: to measure
progress, to mark where the ball must start, or to mark where the game stops.

### Yard lines and numbers: measuring progress

A [**yard line**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-yard-line) is any line across the
field, parallel to the goal lines. Lines are painted every 5 yards, with short ticks at every
single yard along both sidelines and in the two rows of hash marks, and big numbers every 10 yards. The
numbers count *up* from each goal line to the 50 and back down again: there is a 10, 20, 30
and 40 on each half, and only one 50. That's why a broadcaster never says "the 70-yard
line." A spot is named by its distance from the nearer goal line *and* by whose half it's in:
"first down at their own 25," "first-and-goal at the Chiefs' 8." The rulebook puts it the same
way: the line 19 yards from team A's goal line is "A's 19," and the line 51 yards from it is
"B's 49." Beside every number except the 50, a small white arrow points toward the nearer goal
line: on a tight camera shot it's the quickest way to tell which side of midfield the ball is on.
The tops of the numbers, about 14 yards in from each sideline, are also a landmark
receivers line up on, which you'll meet as
[the numbers](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-02-formation-rules-and-vocabulary.qmd).

Why paint so much? Because almost every rule that matters is a distance: how far the offense
must go to keep the ball, where a penalty is enforced, where the next play starts. The
grid lets 22 players, 7 officials and a television audience agree on where the ball is, to
the yard, without a tape measure. The basic bargain, in one sentence: the offense gets four
tries, called *downs*, to move the ball 10 yards; make it and it earns a fresh set (a *first
down*), fail on *fourth down* and the ball goes to the other team. Every play starts from the
*line of scrimmage*, the yard line where the ball sits before the snap; any snapped play (a run,
a pass, a punt or a field-goal try, but not a kickoff) is a *play from scrimmage*. All of that, plus the
yellow line you see on TV, is the subject of
[Downs, Distance, and Field Position](01-02-downs-distance-and-field-position.qmd).

### End zone, goal line, end line

The [**end zone**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-end-zone) is the 10-yard-deep box at
each end, between the **goal line** and the **end line**. An offense scores by getting the
ball into the end zone it is attacking, and it defends the one behind it. The
[**goal line**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-goal-line) is the line between the field of
play and the end zone, and it has one property that surprises most new fans: **the goal line
is part of the end zone.** A ball carried *onto* the goal line is already a touchdown. Officials
talk about the ball "breaking the plane": the goal line is treated as an invisible wall
rising straight up from the paint, and the moment any part of the ball, in a runner's
control, touches that wall, the play is over and six points go on the board. The orange
pylons at the four corners of each end zone are in the end zone too, so a ball carried over
or inside a pylon counts.[^plane]

The goal posts stand on the end line, at the *back* of the end zone. Their crossbar is 10 feet
off the ground, the uprights are 18 feet 6 inches apart and rise 35 feet above the
crossbar.[^posts] They haven't always been there; we'll see why they moved when we get to the
field goal.

### Sidelines: where the game stops

A [**sideline**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-sideline) is one of the two long boundary
lines. Together with the end lines, the sidelines enclose the playing surface, and a solid
white border at least 6 feet wide runs outside them. Here is the rule that matters more than
any other on this page: **the sideline is out of bounds.** So is the end line. A runner who
puts one toe on the white paint is out of bounds, and the play ends where the ball was when he
did it. The goal line is in, the boundary lines are out. Here are the edge cases.

```{python}
#| label: fig-in-or-out
#| fig-cap: "The goal line is in; the sideline and end line are out. A close-up of one corner of an end zone, offense attacking up the page. Only the ball counts for a touchdown (cases 1 to 4), but for out of bounds, any part of the player counts (cases 5 and 6)."
fig = plt.figure(figsize=(6.5, 4.3))
gs = fig.add_gridspec(1, 2, width_ratios=[1.0, 1.25], wspace=0.02)
axk = fig.add_subplot(gs[0]); blank(axk)
ax = fig.add_subplot(gs[1])
fld = Field(ax=ax, orient="vertical", los=90, window=(10, 30), to_go=None, lateral=(0.0, 21.0))
field_extras(fld, posts=False, try_lines=False, pylon_size=0.9)
P = fld.xy
x_lo, _ = ax.get_xlim(); y_lo, _ = ax.get_ylim()
ax.set_xlim(x_lo, FIELD_WIDTH + 3.6); ax.set_ylim(y_lo, 123.2)
ax.text(*P(103.0, -2.45), "out of bounds", rotation=90, fontsize=6.5, ha="center", va="center", color=style.INK_2)
ax.text(*P(121.5, 12.0), "out of bounds", fontsize=6.5, ha="center", va="center", color=style.INK_2)
ax.text(*P(115.0, 12.0), "END ZONE", fontsize=11, ha="center", va="center", color=style.MUTED, alpha=0.6,
        fontweight="bold")
ax.text(*P(107.5, 15.5), "field of play", fontsize=8, ha="center", va="center", color=style.MUTED)
ax.text(*P(109.7, 20.6), "goal line", fontsize=6.5, ha="left", va="top", color=style.INK_2)
ax.text(*P(101.0, 0.9), "sideline", rotation=90, fontsize=6.5, ha="center", va="bottom", color=style.INK_2)
gx, gy = P([110, 110], [0, 21])
ax.plot(gx, gy, color=style.INK_2, lw=2.2, zorder=2)          # the goal line, painted IN the end zone

cases = [(1, (110.35, 15.0), 90, True), (2, (110.0, 9.5), 90, True), (3, (109.25, 4.5), 90, False),
         (4, (110.3, 0.35), 60, True), (5, (106.0, 0.0), 90, False), (6, (120.0, 6.0), 90, False)]
offs = {1: (-1.6, 1.7), 2: (-1.6, 1.7), 3: (0.0, -2.0), 4: (-1.0, 2.0), 5: (-2.0, 0.0), 6: (-2.0, 0.0)}
for num, (bx, by), ang, good in cases:
    px, py = (float(v) for v in P(bx, by))
    if num in (5, 6):   # a foot touching a boundary line
        ax.add_patch(Ellipse((px, py), 0.9, 1.6, facecolor=style.INK, edgecolor="white", lw=0.6, zorder=12))
    else:
        football(ax, px, py, w=1.5, h=0.9, angle=ang)
    if num == 3:        # his shoulder is over the line, the ball is not
        draw_marker(ax, *(float(v) for v in P(110.7, 4.5)), "off", "", 10, r=0.8)
        sx, sy = (float(v) for v in P(110.7, 4.5))
        callout(ax, "his shoulder", (sx - 0.8, sy), (sx - 4.6, sy - 2.6), fs=6.2)
    col = style.THIRD if good else style.DEFENSE_DARK
    ax.text(px + offs[num][0], py + offs[num][1], str(num), fontsize=8, fontweight="bold", color="white",
            ha="center", va="center", zorder=13, bbox=dict(boxstyle="circle,pad=0.18", fc=col, ec="none"))
clip_texts(ax)

key = [(True, "Touchdown.", "Any part of the ball, held by a runner, breaks the plane of the goal line."),
       (True, "Touchdown.", "The ball is on the line. The goal line belongs to the end zone."),
       (False, "Not yet.", "His shoulder is over the line, but the ball is short of it. Only the ball counts."),
       (True, "Touchdown.", "Ball over the pylon. The pylon is in the end zone too (a ball that crosses outside the pylon is out of bounds)."),
       (False, "Out of bounds.", "A foot on the sideline: he is out where the ball was, at the 4."),
       (False, "Incomplete.", "A receiver's foot on the end line. The end line is out of bounds.")]
y = 0.97
for i, (good, head, body) in enumerate(key, 1):
    col = style.THIRD if good else style.DEFENSE_DARK
    axk.text(0.02, y, str(i), transform=axk.transAxes, fontsize=8, fontweight="bold", color="white",
             ha="center", va="top", bbox=dict(boxstyle="circle,pad=0.18", fc=col, ec="none"))
    axk.text(0.09, y + 0.004, head, transform=axk.transAxes, fontsize=8, fontweight="bold", color=style.INK,
             ha="left", va="top")
    lines = textwrap.wrap(body, 34)
    axk.text(0.09, y - 0.045, "\n".join(lines), transform=axk.transAxes, fontsize=7.2,
             color=style.INK_2, ha="left", va="top", linespacing=1.2)
    y -= 0.085 + 0.041 * len(lines)
plt.show()
```

The asymmetry is deliberate. The end zone is a reward, so the rules are generous about
reaching it: the ball only has to *touch* the plane. The sidelines are a limit, so the rules
are strict about crossing them: a toenail on the paint is enough. Notice also that the two tests
look at different things. For a touchdown, only the ball matters, so a runner can be falling
out of bounds and still score if the ball crossed the plane first (case 4). For out of bounds,
the *player* matters: if any part of him touches the line while he holds the ball, the ball is
out at that spot, even if the ball itself is still over the field.

::: {.callout-caution title="Common misconception"}
"He has to get into the end zone." A *runner* doesn't: only the ball does, which is why you
see backs stretch the ball out over the goal line while their bodies are being driven backward.
A *receiver* catching a pass in the end zone is different. He has to complete the catch with
both feet (or a knee, hip or elbow) down in bounds, which is why the toe-tap along the back
line gets reviewed so often. What counts as a catch is its own small body of law; it's in
[Officiating, Replay, and the Rules of the Ball](../09-special-teams-and-the-rules-that-shape-strategy/09-04-officiating-replay-and-rules-of-the-ball.qmd).
:::

## Hash marks: where every play starts

Look down the middle of the field and you'll see two rows of short dashes running its whole
length. These are the [**hash marks**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-hash-marks) (the
rulebook calls them *inbounds lines*), and in the NFL they sit 70 feet 9 inches in from each
sideline, which leaves them 18 feet 6 inches apart. That gap is exactly the width
of the goal posts, and that's no accident, as you'll see below.

The rule that makes them matter is simple. **Every play from scrimmage starts with the ball on
or between the hash marks.** If a play ends between them, the next one starts where the ball
was declared dead. If it ends outside them, say a runner is tackled 4 yards from the
sideline or runs out of bounds, the officials carry the ball in to the nearer hash. So most
snaps start on one hash or the other, and the ball's position across the field changes from
play to play. Watch for it: the camera will show the ball sitting on the left or the right
hash far more often than dead center. There are two exceptions. On the try after a touchdown and
on the first snap after a touchback, the offense may put the ball anywhere on or between the
hashes, so a team can snap its extra point from wherever its kicker likes best.[^spot]

### Why it exists: the indoor game of 1932

The NFL didn't always have hash marks. Before 1933, the next play generally started where the
last one ended, so a runner tackled a yard from the sideline left his team snapping the ball a
yard from the sideline, with almost no room on one side of the formation. Teams were stuck with a
lopsided formation and often spent a play just running back toward the middle to get room back.
The fix came from an accident. The 1932 season ended with the Chicago Bears and the Portsmouth
Spartans tied for first, and a blizzard drove the playoff game indoors to Chicago Stadium, onto
a makeshift field only 80 yards long and 30 feet narrower than normal, with the stands right up
against the sidelines. A special rule for that game let the ball be moved in from the walls after
plays that ended near them (accounts differ on the details). The game worked so well that for
1933 the league wrote the idea into the rulebook: the ball would be spotted on the hash marks on
every play.[^firstplayoff]

The hashes then crept toward the middle of the field. They were 10 yards from the sidelines in
1933, 15 yards from 1935, 20 yards from 1945, and in 1972 the NFL moved them to 23 yards, 1 foot
and 9 inches, the same width as the goal posts.[^hash72] Each move gave the offense more room
to the short side and made the field more symmetrical. The 1972 change was made to help
offenses after a drop in scoring, one of a string of 1970s rule changes with the same aim, a
story told in
[From the Single Wing to the Scoring Drought](../11-history/11-01-single-wing-to-scoring-drought.qmd).[^offense72]

### Field side and boundary side

When the ball is on a hash, it is no longer in the middle of the field, so the two sides of the
formation are different sizes. The side with more room is the
[**field side**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-field-side), also called the
[**wide side**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-wide-side). The side closer to the sideline
is the [**boundary side**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-boundary-side), or
[**short side**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-short-side). In the NFL the difference is
23.6 yards versus 29.8 yards: about 6 yards. When the ball is in the middle of the field,
neither side is the field side, and teams use some other rule to decide which way to call
things, usually the side with more receivers (the formation's *strength*, built out in
[Formation Rules and Vocabulary](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-02-formation-rules-and-vocabulary.qmd)).

Six yards may not sound like much, but with eleven players a side, the sideline acts like a
twelfth defender: a runner or receiver headed toward it runs out of room, and the defense can use
it to trap him. The difference matters most for plays that stretch to the edge (sweeps, throws
toward the sideline, screens to the outside) and hardly at all for plays between the hashes. So
the hash changes the plan on both sides of the ball:

- **Offense.** Plays that need room to run sideways (sweeps, wide runs, screens to the
  outside, receivers breaking toward the sideline) usually go to the field. Throws to the
  boundary are shorter, because the quarterback is closer to that sideline, so quick throws
  outside are safer there. Many offenses line up most of their receivers to the wide side so
  they have room to spread out, and leave one receiver alone to the boundary.
- **Defense.** Many defenses assign roles by side rather than by left and right: a "field
  corner" and a "boundary corner," a field safety and a boundary safety. The boundary corner
  can play more aggressively, because the sideline takes away his outside; the field corner
  has acres to defend. So teams that play this way cast the parts to fit: the boundary corner is
  often the bigger, more physical player who presses and tackles, the field corner the better
  cover man in space, and the boundary safety the one who comes up to stop the run. When the
  offense stacks receivers to the wide side, these defenses slide their safeties that way too,
  leaving the boundary corner alone against the single receiver. This is mostly a college habit:
  with the NFL's narrow hashes, many pro defenses set their calls by the formation's strength
  instead. Playing a different coverage to each side is a whole family of schemes, which you'll
  meet in [Disguise, Rotation, and Split-Field Coverage](../06-pass-coverage/06-06-disguise-rotation-and-split-field.qmd).
- **Kickers.** A field goal is snapped from wherever the last play ended, so one from a hash is
  kicked at a slight angle. Because NFL hashes are only as wide as the uprights, the angle is
  mild, which is one reason NFL teams rarely spend a down centering the ball (running a play
  toward the middle so it is spotted there) before a kick, a habit you'll see more in college.

### NFL versus college versus high school

The hash marks are the biggest difference between the fields you see on Saturday and Sunday.
College hashes are 40 feet apart, 60 feet from each sideline; high school hashes are 53 feet 4
inches apart, splitting the field into thirds.[^collegehash] The fields are the same size. The
only thing that changes is where the ball can start.

The next picture is the chapter's first with players in it, so here is how to read every
diagram in this book. Blue circles are the offense, orange squares the defense, and the offense
always moves up the page (or, in a wide picture, to the right). The letters name positions:
Q is the quarterback, R a running back, and X, Z, H and Y are receivers. The five blank circles
in a row are the offensive linemen. You don't need the letters yet; they're decoded in
[The Twenty-Two](01-03-the-twenty-two.qmd).

```{python}
#| label: fig-hash-compare
#| fig-cap: "The same four-receiver formation (two receivers on each side) with the ball on the left hash, on three sets of hash marks. Receivers line up by landmarks, not by fixed distances from the ball: the receiver to the short side (X) won't stand much closer than about 7 yards to the sideline, so he has room to run toward it. On the NFL field (23.6 yards to one sideline, 29.8 to the other) he can stand at his normal spot. On the college and high-school fields he has to cut in toward the ball, squeezing everything on the short side, while the wide side has more room than anyone can use."
LEVELS = [("NFL", HASH_NEAR, "hashes 18 ft 6 in apart (the width of the goal posts)"),
          ("College", 20.0, "hashes 40 ft apart"),
          ("High school", FIELD_WIDTH / 3, "hashes 53 ft 4 in apart: the field split in thirds")]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(3, 1, figsize=(6.5, 5.9))
for ax, (name, near, sub) in zip(axes, LEVELS):
    far = FIELD_WIDTH - near
    x_w = -min(15.0, near - 7.0)               # X: on his normal spot, or 7 yd off the sideline
    off = [q.moved(w=x_w) if q.key == "X" else q.moved(w=x_w * 0.6) if q.key == "H" else q
           for q in ch1(offense("gun_2x2"))]
    with hashes_at(near):
        p = Play(off, None, los=40, ball_y=far, to_go=None)
        fld = p.draw(ax=ax, window=(-6.5, 7.0), lateral="full", title=False)
    P = fld.xy
    hide_numbers(ax)              # the yard-line numbers would sit on top of the formation here
    for (y0, y1, side) in [(far, FIELD_WIDTH, "short (boundary) side"), (0.0, far, "wide (field) side")]:
        (ax0, ay0), (ax1, ay1) = P(43.5, y0), P(43.5, y1)
        ax.annotate("", xy=(float(ax0), float(ay0)), xytext=(float(ax1), float(ay1)),
                    arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="<->", color=style.INK_2, lw=0.9), zorder=9)
        ax.text((float(ax0) + float(ax1)) / 2, float(ay0) + 0.9, f"{side}: {abs(y1 - y0):.1f} yd", fontsize=7.5,
                ha="center", va="bottom", color=style.INK, zorder=10,
                bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.15", fc=style.SURFACE, ec="none", alpha=0.9))
    for key in ("X", "Z"):                     # room outside each outside receiver
        pl = p.players[key]
        bx, by = (float(v) for v in P(*p.to_abs(pl.d, pl.w)))
        edge = 0.0 if key == "X" else FIELD_WIDTH
        x_in = bx - 1.0 if key == "X" else bx + 1.0
        ax.annotate("", xy=(x_in, by - 2.2), xytext=(edge + (0.2 if key == "X" else -0.2), by - 2.2),
                    arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="<->", color=style.INK_2, lw=0.8), zorder=9)
        ax.text(edge + (1.6 if key == "X" else -1.6), by - 3.0, f"{abs(bx - edge):.0f} yd outside {key}",
                fontsize=6.5, ha="left" if key == "X" else "right", va="top", color=style.INK_2, zorder=10)
    xb, yb = (float(v) for v in P(*p.to_abs(0.0, x_w)))
    ax.text(xb + 1.5, yb + 2.4, f"X is {abs(x_w):.0f} yd from the ball", fontsize=6.5, ha="left", va="bottom",
            color=style.INK, zorder=10, bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.12", fc=style.SURFACE, ec="none", alpha=0.9))
    ax.text(0.0, 1.02, name, transform=ax.transAxes, fontsize=9.5, fontweight="bold", color=style.INK,
            ha="left", va="bottom")
    ax.text(0.16 if name != "High school" else 0.22, 1.02, sub, transform=ax.transAxes, fontsize=7.5,
            color=style.INK_2, ha="left", va="bottom")
fig.subplots_adjust(hspace=0.32, left=0.01, right=0.99, top=0.95, bottom=0.01)
plt.show()
```

This one measurement explains a lot of the difference between college and pro offense. A
college offense with the ball on the hash has a huge wide side to attack and a cramped short
side, so the field itself tells everyone where the space is, and college schemes lean hard on
"to the field" and "into the boundary" rules. An NFL field is close to symmetrical, so
alignment and play design depend less on the hash and more on the formation and the defense.
It's also why an NFL quarterback has to make the throw outside to *both* sides of the field:
there is no cramped short side where every throw toward the sideline is a short toss, and the boundary throw is
almost as long as the field throw.
The college game as the sport's laboratory is a recurring thread in
[The College Laboratory](../11-history/11-03-the-college-laboratory.qmd).

## Scoring: five ways onto the scoreboard

There are only five ways to score, and three of them come in a bundle: the touchdown and the
two kinds of try that follow it.[^scorevalues]

Four happen at the end the offense is attacking (the touchdown is shown as a run in progress; the two tries start between the hash marks, where the offense chooses). The safety happens at the other end, in the offense's own end zone, and it counts for the defense.
