### Touchdown: six points

A [**touchdown**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-touchdown) is worth six points. The
offense scores one by running the ball across the goal line, or by catching a pass in the end
zone. The defense or a kick-return team can score one too, by intercepting a pass or picking up
a fumble and returning it all the way, or by returning a kick. Any recovery of a loose ball in
the opponent's end zone also counts. The touchdown is the point of the whole enterprise, and it
is not easy: in 2025, only `{python} f"{td_share:.0%}"` of the times an NFL team got the ball
ended with one.

### The try: one point or two

After every touchdown, the scoring team gets one more snap, called the *try*, and the clock
doesn't run during it. It's played even if time ran out on the touchdown, and skipped only when
it can't matter, as after a touchdown that wins the game in overtime. The team chooses between
two very different plays:

- The [**extra point**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-extra-point) (also the
  [**PAT**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-pat), for "point after touchdown") is a kick
  through the uprights worth one point. Since 2015 it has been snapped from the 15-yard line,
  so the kick itself, from about the 23, is about 33 yards.[^xp2015]
- The [**two-point conversion**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-two-point-conversion) is
  one ordinary play from the 2-yard line: run or pass the ball into the end zone and you get
  two points. The NFL adopted it only in 1994; the old AFL had used it in the 1960s and college
  football since 1958.[^twopt]

On the try the defense can score too: if it blocks the kick, or intercepts or recovers on a
two-point try, and returns the ball the length of the field, it gets two points. That rule also
dates from 2015.

Why have two options at all? Because they are worth almost exactly the same on average, which
makes the choice depend on the *score*, not on the play.

```{python}
#| label: fig-try-value
#| fig-cap: "Average points per try, NFL regular seasons 2010–2025: the success rate times the points. Before 2015 the extra point, kicked from the 2, was a near-certain 1 point. Moving it back to the 15 cut its success to about 93–96%. The two-point try succeeds roughly half the time, so it is worth about the same; it bounces from year to year because there are only about 90–150 attempts a season."
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 3.0))
ax.plot(xp_rate.index, xp_rate.values, color=style.SERIES[2], marker="o", ms=3.5,
        label="Extra-point kick (1 point × success rate)")
ax.plot(tp_rate.index, 2 * tp_rate.values, color=style.SERIES[1], marker="o", ms=3.5,
        label="Two-point try (2 points × success rate)")
ax.axvline(2014.5, color=style.MUTED, lw=1, ls=(0, (3, 2)))
ax.text(2014.6, 1.13, "2015: kick moved\nback to the 15", fontsize=7.5, color=style.INK_2, ha="left", va="top")
ax.set_ylim(0.75, 1.15)
ax.set_ylabel("average points per try")
ax.set_xticks(range(2010, 2026, 3))
ax.legend(loc="lower left", fontsize=7.5)
plt.show()
```

The chart shows the history.[^trycalc] For most of football history the extra point was close
to automatic: `{python} f"{xp_rate.loc[2014]:.1%}"` of kicks were good in 2014, when the ball
was snapped from the 2 and the kick was a 20-yarder. A play that is always successful isn't a
decision, and the league moved the kick back to make it one. It worked a little: success fell to
`{python} f"{xp_rate.loc[2015]:.1%}"` the next season, and teams more than doubled their two-point
attempts, from about `{python} f"{tp_att.loc[2010:2014].mean():.0f}"` a season before the change
to about `{python} f"{tp_att.loc[2021:2025].mean():.0f}"` in 2021–2025. They're still only about
`{python} f"{(tp_att / (tp_att + xp_att)).loc[2021:2025].mean():.0%}"` of all tries, because
when the two options are worth the same, most coaches take the one with less variance.

The real reason to go for two is the scoreboard. A team that trails by 2 after scoring wants
the tie, and only the two-pointer gives it. A team that trails by 8 needs a touchdown *and* a
two-pointer to tie. A team that is down 14 late and scores faces a classic question: kick to
get within 7, or go for two now, so that it knows whether the next touchdown will tie or win?
Analysts have argued that one for a decade; the arithmetic is in chapter 10.

### Field goal: three points from anywhere

A [**field goal**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-field-goal) is worth three points. The
offense snaps the ball back about 7 or 8 yards to a holder, who sets it on the ground, and the
kicker kicks it through the goal posts. It can be tried from anywhere on the field, on any
down, but in practice teams try it on fourth down, when the alternative is giving the ball
away. Because the posts stand on the end line, add about 18 yards to the line of scrimmage to
get the length of the kick: a field goal tried from the opponent's 30 is a 48-yarder. A miss
isn't free. The other team takes over at the spot of the kick, where the holder set the ball
(or at its own 20, if the kick came from inside it), so a missed 53-yarder hands it the ball at
its own 43.[^missedfg]

```{python}
#| label: fig-fg-distance
#| fig-cap: "How often NFL field goals are made, by distance, 2021–2025 regular seasons. Inside 30 yards the kick is close to certain, and from 30–39 yards it is good more than nine times in ten; past 50 it is still made about seven times in ten. That reliability is new: in 2016 and again in 2019, kicks of 50 yards or more were made fewer than six times in ten."
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 2.8))
ax.bar(fg_tab.index.astype(str), fg_tab.made * 100, color=style.SERIES[2], width=0.62)
for i, (n, m) in enumerate(zip(fg_tab.n, fg_tab.made)):
    ax.text(i, m * 100 + 1.5, f"{m:.0%}", ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=8.5, color=style.INK)
    ax.text(i, 4, f"{n:,} kicks", ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=7, color="white")
ax.set_ylim(0, 110); ax.set_yticks([0, 25, 50, 75, 100])
ax.set_ylabel("made (%)"); ax.set_xlabel("kick distance (yards), 2021–2025 regular seasons")
ax.grid(axis="x", visible=False)
plt.show()
```

Modern kickers are remarkable. Kicks from under 30 yards almost never miss, those from 30–39
miss only about one time in fifteen, and kicks of 50 yards or more, made fewer than six times in
ten as recently as 2019, are now made about seven times in ten: in 2025 alone kickers made
`{python} f"{made60_25}"` field goals of 60 yards or more.[^fgcalc] That shifts strategy, because
the farther out a team can count on three points, the sooner a stalled drive still scores.

The goal posts' location is a strategy story too. From 1933 to 1973 the NFL's posts stood *on
the goal line*, at the front of the end zone, a holdover from that same indoor game of 1932.
Field goals were 10 yards shorter, and coaches settled for them constantly. For 1974 the league
moved the posts back to the end line, specifically to make field goals harder and push teams to
play for touchdowns.[^goalposts74] The rules have been nudging coaches away from the three-point
consolation prize for fifty years.

### Safety: two points and the ball

A [**safety**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-safety-score) is the defense's own score:
two points, awarded when the offense's ball carrier is tackled in his own end zone, when the
offense fumbles the ball out of the back or side of its own end zone, or when the offense commits
a foul in its own end zone (most often holding a pass rusher who was about to sack the
quarterback there). The usual picture is a quarterback sacked a yard deep in his own end zone.

The safety comes with a second penalty. The team that gave it up must then *kick the ball
away* from its own 20-yard line, a free kick that is usually punted. So the defense gets two
points **and** the ball, usually near its own 40 (the median first snap after a safety in
2016–2025 was at the scoring team's own `{python} f"{safety_start:.0f}"`). That makes a safety worth more than its two
points suggest, and it's why offenses backed up against their own goal line play so
carefully. Safeties are rare: there were `{python} f"{safeties_25}"` in the whole 2025 regular
season, about one every 23 games.[^safety] (One oddity for trivia night: the rulebook
even allows a *one-point* safety, which can happen only on a try. If a defender intercepts a
two-point pass, runs it out of his own end zone and is tackled back inside it, the offense gets
one point. You will probably never see one.)

The word "safety" also names a defensive position, the deepest defenders on the field. That
one is covered in [The Twenty-Two](01-03-the-twenty-two.qmd).

### Seven versus three: the central tension

Add it up and an NFL score is almost always built from 7s (touchdown plus extra point) and 3s.
The gap between them, **four points**, is the single most important number in football
strategy. It is more than a field goal. A team that settles for a field goal when it could have
scored a touchdown has left more points on the table than it just scored.

```{python}
#| label: fig-drive-outcomes
#| fig-cap: "How every possession ended, 2025 NFL regular season. Fewer than four in ten produced points, and touchdowns outnumbered field goals only about three to two. Defensive and return touchdowns after a turnover are counted with the turnover."
LABEL = {"Touchdown": "Touchdown", "Field goal": "Field goal", "Punt": "Punt",
         "Turnover": "Interception or lost fumble", "Opp touchdown": "Interception or lost fumble",
         "Turnover on downs": "Turnover on downs", "End of half": "Clock ran out (end of half)",
         "Missed field goal": "Missed field goal", "Safety": "Safety"}
share = drives.result.map(LABEL).value_counts(normalize=True).sort_values()
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 3.0))
ax.barh(share.index, share.values * 100, height=0.68,
        color=[style.OFFENSE if k in ("Touchdown", "Field goal") else style.BASELINE for k in share.index])
for i, v in enumerate(share.values * 100):
    ax.text(v + 0.5, i, f"{v:.1f}%", va="center", ha="left", fontsize=8, color=style.INK)
ax.set_xlabel("share of all possessions, 2025 regular season")
ax.grid(axis="y", visible=False)
ax.set_xlim(0, 38)
ax.tick_params(axis="y", length=0, labelsize=8.5, labelcolor=style.INK)
plt.show()
```

Here's why that gap matters so much. A *possession* is one turn with the ball (the next
section is about them), and an NFL team gets only about `{python} f"{per_team_game:.1f}"` of
them a game, scoring about `{python} f"{pts_per_team:.0f}"` points in all (2025 figures).[^drives]
Each one is precious. When a
drive reaches the opponent's 20, the area called the
[red zone](01-02-downs-distance-and-field-position.qmd), it ended in a touchdown
`{python} f"{rz_td:.0%}"` of the time in 2025 and a field goal `{python} f"{rz_fg:.0%}"` of the time. A
team that turns one of those field goals per game into a touchdown gains four points a week;
over a 17-game season that's almost 70 points, the kind of margin that separates an average
team from a playoff team.

So the choice between 7 and 3 runs through every chapter that follows:

- It's why **fourth down near the goal line** is the most second-guessed call in football, and
  why the crowd at the top of this chapter booed the kicker. On fourth down from the 1- or
  2-yard line, a single run or pass scored a touchdown
  `{python} f"{goal_td:.0%}"` of the time in 2016–2025.[^goalline] You'll use that number in the
  third Predict-the-play drill below.
- It's why offenses build whole playbooks for the red zone, where the field shrinks and the
  defense has less ground to cover
  ([Red Zone, Goal Line, and Short Yardage](../10-situational-football/10-03-red-zone-goal-line-and-short-yardage.qmd)).
- It's why a field goal on the opening drive is greeted with a shrug and a touchdown with a
  roar, even though both "scored."

::: {.callout-important title="Why it exists: a scoreboard built from 7s and 3s"}
Because almost all points come in chunks of 7 and 3, some margins matter far more than others.
Leading by 3 means a field goal ties you; by 4, the opponent needs a touchdown; by 8, it needs
a touchdown *and* a two-point conversion; by 9, two scores. Broadcasters call a 9-point lead
"a two-score game" for exactly this reason. The same logic runs up the scale: 14 is two
touchdowns with extra points, 16 is the most two touchdowns can cover (both with two-point
conversions), and at 17 you need three scores. Listen for the margins 3, 7, 8, 14, 16 and 17
late in a game; they're the ones coaches plan around, and they're why a team up by 7 sometimes
kicks a late field goal (to go up 10, two scores) instead of trying for a touchdown.
:::

## Possession: football is a game of turns

Underneath all the scoring is a simpler idea. At any moment one team has
[**possession**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-possession), control of the ball, and
that team is the offense. The other is the defense. Unlike basketball or soccer, the teams don't
swap the ball back and forth in a flowing way; they take *turns*, and each turn (a possession, or
[drive](01-02-downs-distance-and-field-position.qmd)) keeps going until something specific
ends it:

- **The offense scores.** After a touchdown and try, or after a field goal, the scoring team
  *kicks off* (kicks the ball downfield to the other team, described below). This is football's
  built-in fairness: score, and you have to give the ball back.
- **The offense gives it up on purpose,** by punting on fourth down: it trades the ball for 40-odd
  yards of field position rather than handing it over at the line of scrimmage.
- **The offense loses it:** an interception, a lost fumble, failing on fourth down (all
  defined in [Downs, Distance, and Field Position](01-02-downs-distance-and-field-position.qmd)),
  or a missed field goal.
- **The defense scores a safety** and then receives the free kick.
- **The half ends.** Possession does *not* carry across halftime.

The drive-outcome chart above is a census of exactly these endings. With so few turns, each
one is a scarce resource, and that scarcity is what makes the clock matter: a team that can't
stop the clock can't buy itself another turn.

## The shape of a game

```{python}
#| label: fig-game-shape
#| fig-cap: "The shape of an NFL game in game-clock time: four 15-minute quarters, a halftime that resets the kickoff and the timeouts, a two-minute warning near the end of each half, and overtime if the score is tied. Teams switch ends after the first and third quarters but keep the ball, the down and the distance."
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.6, 2.75))
blank(ax); ax.set_xlim(-2, 112); ax.set_ylim(-3, 40)
U = 1.4
starts = {1: 0, 2: 15 * U, 3: 30 * U + 8, 4: 45 * U + 8}
OTX = 60 * U + 8 + 3
for q, x in starts.items():
    ax.add_patch(FancyBboxPatch((x + 0.3, 12), 15 * U - 0.6, 10, boxstyle="round,pad=0,rounding_size=0.8",
                                fc=style.OFFENSE_TINT, ec=style.OFFENSE, lw=1.0, zorder=2))
    ax.text(x + 7.5 * U, 18.6, f"Q{q}", fontsize=10, fontweight="bold", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, ha="center",
            va="center", zorder=3)
    ax.text(x + 7.5 * U, 14.7, "15:00", fontsize=7, color=style.INK_2, ha="center", va="center", zorder=3)
hx = 30 * U
ax.add_patch(FancyBboxPatch((hx + 0.5, 12), 7, 10, boxstyle="round,pad=0,rounding_size=0.8", fc=style.GRID,
                            ec=style.BASELINE, lw=1.0, ls=(0, (3, 2)), zorder=2))
ax.text(hx + 4.0, 17, "half-\ntime", fontsize=6.8, color=style.INK_2, ha="center", va="center", zorder=3,
        linespacing=1.05)
ax.add_patch(FancyBboxPatch((OTX, 12), 13.5, 10, boxstyle="round,pad=0,rounding_size=0.8", fc=style.SURFACE,
                            ec=style.BASELINE, lw=1.0, ls=(0, (3, 2)), zorder=2))
ax.text(OTX + 6.75, 17, "overtime\nif tied", fontsize=7, color=style.INK_2, ha="center", va="center", zorder=3)
for q in (2, 4):
    x = starts[q] + 13 * U
    ax.plot([x, x], [12, 24.5], color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, lw=1.4, zorder=4)
    ax.text(x, 25.3, "two-minute\nwarning", fontsize=6.5, color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, ha="center", va="bottom",
            linespacing=1.05)
for x, lab in ((starts[1], "coin toss,\nkickoff"), (starts[3], "kickoff, usually by\nthe first receivers")):
    ax.add_patch(Polygon([[x + 0.3, 22.4], [x + 2.1, 22.4], [x + 1.2, 24.0]], closed=True, fc=style.THIRD,
                         ec="none", zorder=4))
    ax.text(x + 0.3, 25.3, lab, fontsize=6.5, color=style.INK, ha="left", va="bottom", linespacing=1.05)
for q in (1, 3):
    x = starts[q] + 15 * U
    ax.text(x, 9.5, "⇄", fontsize=11, color=style.INK_2, ha="center", va="center")
    ax.text(x, 6.2, "teams switch ends;\nsame down, distance, spot", fontsize=6.3, color=style.INK_2,
            ha="center", va="top", linespacing=1.05)
for x0, x1, lab in ((starts[1], starts[2] + 15 * U, "first half: each team has 3 timeouts"),
                    (starts[3], starts[4] + 15 * U, "second half: 3 fresh timeouts each")):
    ax.annotate("", xy=(x0 + 0.3, 33.5), xytext=(x1 - 0.3, 33.5),
                arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="|-|,widthA=0.3,widthB=0.3", color=style.INK_2, lw=0.8))
    ax.text((x0 + x1) / 2, 35.3, lab, fontsize=7, color=style.INK, ha="center", va="bottom")
ax.text(hx + 4.0, 9.5, "13 minutes. Nothing\ncarries over: new\nkickoff, new timeouts", fontsize=6.3,
        color=style.INK_2, ha="center", va="top", linespacing=1.05)
ax.text(OTX + 6.75, 9.5, "both teams get\nthe ball; 10 min\n(regular season)", fontsize=6.3, color=style.INK_2,
        ha="center", va="top", linespacing=1.05)
plt.show()
```

**The coin toss.** A few minutes before kickoff the referee tosses a coin at midfield, and
the visiting captain calls it. The winner chooses to kick off or receive, or which goal to
defend, and the loser gets the other choice. For the second half the order flips: the team that
lost the toss gets first choice, and the other team takes the remaining one. The winner can also *defer* his choice to the second half, and most coaches now
do:[^defer] they kick off to start the game and are guaranteed the ball to start the second half.
That matters because the end of a half is when a possession is worth the most. A team that has
the ball as the first half runs out and then receives the second-half kickoff gets two turns in a
row.[^timing]

**The kickoff.** Each half, and every possession after a score, starts with a kickoff: the
kicking team kicks from its own 35-yard line and the other team catches the ball and tries to
run it back. Its rules have changed every season since 2024, which is why it has its own
chapter, [Kickoffs and Returns](../09-special-teams-and-the-rules-that-shape-strategy/09-02-kickoffs-and-returns.qmd).[^kickoff]
For now: a kickoff that lands in the end zone and isn't run out is a
[touchback](../09-special-teams-and-the-rules-that-shape-strategy/09-01-kicking-and-punting.qmd),
and the receiving team starts at its own 35 (the spot since 2025).

**Quarters.** The game is 60 minutes of game-clock time, split into four
[**quarters**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-quarter) of 15 minutes. After the first and
third quarters the teams switch ends, so neither side gets the wind or the sun for a whole
half. Nothing else changes: the same team has the ball, at the mirror-image spot, with the same
down and distance. A drive can run straight through the end of the first or third quarter.

**Halftime.** Between the second and third quarters there's a 13-minute break (much longer at
the Super Bowl, for the show). Halftime is a hard reset. Possession doesn't carry over, unused
timeouts disappear, and the second half starts with a fresh kickoff, usually by the team that
received the first one.

**The two-minute warning.** In the second and fourth quarters, the officials stop the game
after the last play that *started* with more than 2:00 on the clock: the
[**two-minute warning**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-two-minute-warning). Snap at 2:04,
tackle at 1:57, and the warning comes after that play, which is why an offense hurries to get a
snap off just before 2:00. It's an automatic timeout that belongs to neither team, and coaches
count it as a free fourth timeout. It began as a real warning, when official time was kept on
the field rather than on the scoreboard (until 1970); it survives because it's useful, for
strategy and for a guaranteed commercial break at the tensest moment of each half.[^twomin]

**Overtime.** If the score is tied after four quarters, the game goes to overtime, which starts
with a new coin toss. The rules are different for the regular season and the playoffs, and both
changed recently. Since 2025, both teams get at least one possession in regular-season overtime
too (the playoffs adopted this in 2022); after that, the next score wins. Regular-season overtime
is one 10-minute period, and a game still tied after it ends a tie. Playoff overtime uses
15-minute periods and continues until someone wins.[^ot] Until 2022 in the playoffs (2025 in
the regular season), a touchdown on the first possession ended the game; the Chiefs film room below shows the game that changed that, and
overtime strategy is in
[Clock and Game Management](../10-situational-football/10-04-clock-and-game-management.qmd).

Put together, a game is a long chain of turns: about 150 snaps in all, roughly
`{python} f"{scrimmage_per_game:.0f}"` of them runs and passes and the rest kicks.[^plays]
Sixty minutes of clock, about 11 minutes of action, and the clock rules decide how the sixty are
spent.

## The game clock: when it runs and when it stops

The [**game clock**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-game-clock) is the big clock on the
scoreboard and in the corner of your TV, counting down each 15-minute quarter. It is the official
time. It runs during every play, which is no surprise. What surprises people is that it often
keeps running *between* plays too. Whether it does depends entirely on how the last play
ended.[^clockrules]

```{python}
#| label: fig-clock-flow
#| fig-cap: "After this play, is the clock running? Read from the top. The one ending that keeps the clock running is a ball carrier tackled in bounds (including a sack, and including a first down). Every other ending stops it, and the question becomes when it starts again. For a play that goes out of bounds, the answer depends on the time of the game."
RUN_C, STOP_C = "#dff3ea", "#fbe3d9"
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.6, 5.0))
blank(ax); ax.set_xlim(0, 100); ax.set_ylim(0, 76)
box(ax, 50, 71.5, 56, 7, "The play is over. What just happened?", ec=style.INK_2, bold=True, fs=9)
cols = [10, 30, 50, 70, 90]
events = [("Tackled\nin bounds", "runs, sacks, catches;\nfirst downs too"),
          ("Incomplete\npass", "a spike or a\nthrowaway too"),
          ("Out of\nbounds", "runner or receiver\nleaves the field"),
          ("Score or\nturnover", "or any other change\nof possession"),
          ("Timeout,\nflag, injury", "two-minute warning,\nmeasurements too")]
for x, (head, sub) in zip(cols, events):
    ax.plot([50, x], [68, 61.5], color=style.BASELINE, lw=1.0, zorder=1)
    box(ax, x, 54.5, 18.6, 14, head, sub=sub, fs=7.8, sub_fs=5.9, bold=True)
    ax.plot([x, x], [47.5, 44], color=style.BASELINE, lw=1.0, zorder=1)
box(ax, cols[0], 40.5, 18.6, 7, "CLOCK RUNS", fc=RUN_C, ec=style.THIRD, bold=True, fs=7.9)
for x in cols[1:]:
    box(ax, x, 40.5, 18.6, 7, "CLOCK STOPS", fc=STOP_C, ec=style.DEFENSE_DARK, bold=True, fs=7.9)
ax.text(50, 33.4, "When does it start again?", fontsize=8, fontstyle="italic", color=style.INK_2, ha="center",
        va="center", bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.2", fc=style.SURFACE, ec="none"), zorder=3)
for x in cols:
    ax.plot([x, x], [37, 30], color=style.BASELINE, lw=1.0, zorder=1)
box(ax, cols[0], 23.5, 18.6, 13, "Never stopped.", sub="the play clock\nresets to 40", fs=7.3, sub_fs=6.2)
box(ax, cols[1], 23.5, 18.6, 13, "On the snap.", sub="which is why a spike\n'stops the clock'", fs=7.3, sub_fs=6.2)
box(ax, cols[2], 23.5, 18.6, 13, "Late in a half?", sub="after the 1st-half\n2:00 warning, or\nunder 5:00 in the 2nd",
    fs=7.3, sub_fs=5.8)
box(ax, cols[3], 23.5, 18.6, 13, "On the snap,", sub="or, after a kickoff,\nwhen a returner\ntouches the ball",
    fs=7.3, sub_fs=6.0)
box(ax, cols[4], 23.5, 18.6, 13, "It depends.", sub="timeout: on the snap.\nflag, injury: often\nas if it hadn't",
    fs=7.3, sub_fs=5.8)
ax.plot([cols[2], 39.5], [17, 12.2], color=style.BASELINE, lw=1.0)
ax.plot([cols[2], 60.5], [17, 12.2], color=style.BASELINE, lw=1.0)
ax.text(cols[2] - 7.0, 15.4, "yes", fontsize=6.5, color=style.INK_2, ha="center")
ax.text(cols[2] + 7.0, 15.4, "no", fontsize=6.5, color=style.INK_2, ha="center")
box(ax, 39.5, 6.8, 19.5, 10.5, "Yes: on the snap.", sub="late-game time is\nprotected", fs=7.0, sub_fs=6.1)
box(ax, 60.5, 6.8, 19.5, 10.5, "No: on the ready.", sub="the referee re-spots\nthe ball and winds it", fs=7.0,
    sub_fs=6.1)
plt.show()
```

Walk through it once and the logic becomes obvious:

- **A ball carrier tackled in bounds: the clock keeps running.** That includes a quarterback
  sacked behind the line and, in the NFL, a play that gains a first down. The officials need a
  few seconds to spot the ball, and those seconds tick away.
- **An incomplete pass stops the clock**, and it stays stopped until the next snap. This is why
  a quarterback in a hurry will *spike* the ball, throwing it straight into the turf the moment
  it's snapped: it's an intentional incomplete pass that buys a stopped clock for the price of
  a down (more in [Clock and Game Management](../10-situational-football/10-04-clock-and-game-management.qmd)).
- **Out of bounds stops the clock**, but for most of the game only briefly. Normally, once the
  officials have put the ball back on the hash and the referee signals it's ready for play, the
  clock starts again, well before the snap. But after the two-minute warning of the first half,
  and in the last five minutes of the game, it stays stopped until the snap. That exception,
  the [out-of-bounds clock rule](../10-situational-football/10-04-clock-and-game-management.qmd),
  is why the broadcaster praised the receiver who got out of bounds in the opening scene, and why
  a defense protecting a late lead tries so hard to tackle receivers *inside* the field.
- **Any score or change of possession stops the clock.** After a score it starts again on the
  kickoff, but only when someone legally touches the ball in the field of play, so a kickoff
  that ends in a touchback takes no time at all. After a turnover or punt it starts on the
  next snap.
- **A timeout, a penalty flag, an injury, the two-minute warning or a measurement for a first
  down** all stop it. When it restarts varies: after a team timeout or the two-minute warning,
  on the snap; after most flags and injuries, the clock starts again as if the stoppage hadn't
  happened (so if it was running, it runs again when the ball is ready). Late in each half the
  rules tighten, so that a team can't use a deliberate foul or a fake injury to save time; a team
  that does can be charged a
  [10-second runoff](../10-situational-football/10-04-clock-and-game-management.qmd), ten
  seconds taken straight off the clock.

```{python}
#| label: fig-clock-two-plays
#| fig-cap: "Same gain, two different clocks. Both receivers (X, outlined) catch the ball 12 yards downfield for a first down. On the left, the out route takes him to the sideline and he steps out: the clock stops. On the right, the dig takes him over the middle, where the corner (C) and the Will linebacker (W) tackle him in bounds: the clock keeps running while everyone hurries back to the line."
def clock_play(kind):
    dfn = [Player("CB", "CB", "def", 7.0, -15.5, label="C"), Player("WILL", "WILL", "def", 5.5, -5.0, label="W")]
    p = Play(offense("gun_2x2"), dfn, los=55, to_go=10)
    p.dropback(1.0)
    if kind == "out":
        p.route("X", r.out(12, 6))
        p.pass_to("X", t=2.0)
        p.run("X", [(0.6, -5.4)])                          # turns upfield and steps out of bounds
        p.path("CB", [(12.8, -24.5)], absolute=True)
        p.note("caught at +12,\nsteps out of bounds", at=(17.0, -19.5))
        p.note("CLOCK STOPS", at=(20.6, -12.0))
    else:
        p.route("X", r.dig(12, 8))
        p.pass_to("X", t=2.0)
        p.run("X", [(0.8, 1.2)])
        p.path("CB", [(12.3, -8.2)], absolute=True)
        p.path("WILL", [(12.6, -3.6)], absolute=True)
        p.note("caught at +12 (a first down),\ntackled in bounds", at=(17.0, -12.0))
        p.note("CLOCK RUNS", at=(20.6, -12.0))
    p.highlight("X")
    return p


fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.6, 4.1))
for ax, kind, title in zip(axes, ("out", "dig"), ("Out route to the sideline", "Dig route over the middle")):
    p = clock_play(kind)
    fld = p.draw(ax=ax, window=(-7, 23.5), lateral=(-26.67, 5.0), title=False)
    P = fld.xy
    (x0, y0), (x1, y1) = P(55 - 7, FIELD_WIDTH), P(55 + 23.5, FIELD_WIDTH + 2.4)   # out-of-bounds border
    lo, hi = sorted([float(x0), float(x1)])
    ax.add_patch(Rectangle((lo, min(float(y0), float(y1))), hi - lo, abs(float(y1) - float(y0)),
                           facecolor=BORDER, edgecolor="none", zorder=0.8))
    ax.set_xlim(lo - 0.3, ax.get_xlim()[1])
    clip_texts(ax)
    ax.set_title(title, fontsize=9, fontweight="bold", color=style.INK, loc="left")
fig.subplots_adjust(wspace=0.04, left=0.01, right=0.99, top=0.93, bottom=0.01)
plt.show()
```

Once you see the clock this way, a lot of late-game football explains itself. A team that is
**behind** wants the clock stopped, so it throws passes (an incompletion stops the clock too)
and aims for the sidelines. A team that is **ahead** wants the clock running, so it runs the
ball, keeps its receivers in bounds, and takes as long as the rules allow between snaps. The
trailing team's defense will even let a runner gain a few extra yards rather than give up a
tackle in bounds that keeps the clock moving. Late in a close game, almost every call is a
clock call as much as a yardage call. Coaches have names for the two modes, the *two-minute
drill* and the *four-minute offense*, and both are built out in
[Clock and Game Management](../10-situational-football/10-04-clock-and-game-management.qmd).

::: {.callout-caution title="Common misconception"}
"The clock stops on a first down." Not in the NFL, and that's a habit carried over from college
football, where for decades the clock stopped briefly after every first down. Even college
dropped that in 2023, except in the last two minutes of each half, to shorten games.[^ncaa] In the
NFL a first down doesn't stop the clock. The chains move and the clock keeps running.
:::

### Timeouts

A [**timeout**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-timeout) is a stoppage a team asks for.
The head coach or any player on the field can call one. Each team gets **three per half**, and
unused first-half timeouts don't carry into the second half; in regular-season overtime each
team gets two.[^timeouts] A timeout stops the game clock at once, and the clock then starts
again on the next snap.

Teams use timeouts for three different jobs, and good coaches know which job they're paying
for:

1. **To stop the clock** late in a half, when time is worth more than anything. This is the
   most valuable use, and the reason announcers count a team's remaining timeouts aloud in the
   final minutes. Each one is worth roughly 40 seconds that would otherwise have run off
   between plays.
2. **To avoid a penalty or a bad play**, when the play clock is about to hit zero, the wrong
   players are on the field, or the quarterback doesn't like what the defense is showing.
3. **To talk**, or to make the other team think: a defense can call one just before a
   field-goal attempt to make the kicker wait (only once per kick; a second try is a penalty).

The tension is that jobs 2 and 3 spend the resource job 1 needs. A team that burns two timeouts
on substitution mix-ups in the third quarter may have nothing left when it needs to stop the
clock at the end of the game.

## The play clock: forty seconds between snaps

The game clock isn't the only clock. A second one, the [**play
clock**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-play-clock), counts down the time between plays;
you'll see it in the corner of the screen and on posts above each end zone. When a play ends,
it starts at **40 seconds**, and the offense must snap the ball before it reaches zero. If it
doesn't, it's a five-yard [delay of game](01-04-what-a-play-really-is.qmd) penalty. After
certain administrative stoppages (a timeout, a change of possession, a penalty enforcement, the
two-minute warning, the start of a quarter) the play clock starts at **25 seconds** instead, once
the referee has spotted the ball and blown his whistle.[^playclock]

::: {.callout-important title="Why it exists: two clocks, two jobs"}
The two clocks measure different things. The **game clock** measures how much *football* is
left. The **play clock** keeps the game moving by limiting how long an offense can stand around
between snaps. The 25-second version exists because after a long stoppage both teams already
know what's coming and have had time to talk, so there's no need to give them 40 more seconds;
the 40-second version starts the instant a play ends, so it already covers the time it takes to
get up, unpile and walk back.
:::

Most of the time the two clocks run together, and that combination is the most important
arithmetic in late-game football. If the game clock is running, every snap can burn up to 40
seconds of it, plus however long the play itself takes. A team with the lead and a fresh set
of downs can simply have its quarterback kneel down three times, letting the play clock run
nearly to zero before each snap, and drain about two minutes without risking a fumble; that's
the *victory formation* you see to end so many games, covered in
[Clock and Game Management](../10-situational-football/10-04-clock-and-game-management.qmd).
The trailing team's only defense is to stop the game clock, and its timeouts are the only tool it
has. So "they have three timeouts left" really means "they can stop the bleeding three times."

The play clock also shapes everything that happens *before* a play. Choosing the play, sending
it in, huddling, lining up and reading the defense all have to fit inside those 40 seconds, and
the coach's radio to the quarterback even cuts out with 15 seconds left. That chain is the
subject of [What a Play Really Is](01-04-what-a-play-really-is.qmd), and what the offense does
in the final seconds before the snap is
[The Pre-Snap Phase](01-05-the-pre-snap-phase.qmd).

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Chiefs 2021 — thirteen seconds"}
The most famous lesson in clock rules came in the AFC Divisional round on January 23, 2022
(the 2021 season), Buffalo at Kansas City. The last two minutes produced three touchdowns.
Buffalo went ahead 29–26 with 1:54 left; Kansas City answered with a 64-yard touchdown by Tyreek
Hill to lead 33–29; and Josh Allen's 19-yard touchdown pass to Gabriel Davis and the extra point
put the Bills back ahead, 36–33, with **13 seconds** left.[^thirteen]

Then three clock details decided the game:

1. **The kickoff took no time.** Buffalo's kicker boomed the ball into the end zone for a
   touchback. Because the clock only starts when the ball is touched in the field of play, the
   Chiefs started at their own 25 with all 13 seconds still on the clock.
2. **Two completions in bounds, two timeouts.** Patrick Mahomes hit Tyreek Hill for 19 yards
   (the clock ran from 0:13 to 0:08, and Kansas City called timeout), then Travis Kelce for 25
   yards to the Bills' 31 (0:08 to 0:03, timeout). Neither receiver went out of bounds, which
   didn't matter: Kansas City had timeouts to spend, and spent them.
3. **A 49-yard field goal at 0:03** by Harrison Butker, from the 31 (31 + 18), tied it 36–36.

Kansas City won the overtime coin toss, drove the length of the field, and won 42–36 on Mahomes's
8-yard touchdown pass to Kelce. Under the rules then in force, that first-possession touchdown
ended the game; Allen never touched the ball in overtime. The league changed playoff overtime for
the next season so that both teams get a possession, and in 2025 extended that to the regular
season.

What to notice: thirteen seconds was enough because of *where* the plays happened and *what the
Chiefs had left*. Two timeouts plus a kickoff that didn't run the clock turned 13 seconds into
three snaps. Buffalo's options were a short kick to make Kansas City return it (burning time) or
coverage that kept everything in front, and both are now standard talking points in exactly that
situation.
:::

## Film room: Super Bowl LIX on one field

Every type of score except the safety showed up in a single game: Super Bowl LIX, February 9,
2025, at the Caesars Superdome in New Orleans, the Eagles' 40–22 win over the Chiefs that ended
the 2024 season.[^lix] Here is every scoring play, located on the field.

```{python}
#| label: fig-lix-scoring
#| fig-cap: "Super Bowl LIX, every scoring play, each drawn with the scoring team attacking left to right (in the real game the teams switched ends every quarter). Solid lines are touchdowns, starting at the line of scrimmage; the green line is Cooper DeJean's interception return, starting where he caught the ball; dashed lines are field goals, starting at the spot of the hold. The running score is at the right. Data: nflverse play-by-play."
PHI = [("Q1 6:18", "Hurts 1-yd run (tush push)", "td", 1, "7–0"),
       ("Q2 8:42", "Elliott 48-yd field goal", "fg", 48, "10–0"),
       ("Q2 7:16", "DeJean 38-yd interception return", "ret", 38, "17–0"),
       ("Q2 1:40", "Hurts 12-yd pass to A.J. Brown", "td", 12, "24–0"),
       ("Q3 5:22", "Elliott 29-yd field goal", "fg", 29, "27–0"),
       ("Q3 2:47", "Hurts 46-yd pass to DeVonta Smith", "td", 46, "34–0"),
       ("Q4 9:56", "Elliott 48-yd field goal", "fg", 48, "37–6"),
       ("Q4 8:05", "Elliott 50-yd field goal", "fg", 50, "40–6")]
KC = [("Q3 0:43", "Mahomes 24-yd pass to Worthy", "td", 24, "6–34", "2-pt try fails"),
      ("Q4 2:58", "Mahomes 7-yd pass to Hopkins", "td", 7, "14–40", "2-pt try good"),
      ("Q4 1:56", "Mahomes 50-yd pass to Worthy", "td", 50, "22–40", "2-pt try good")]

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(6.6, 4.75),
                         gridspec_kw=dict(height_ratios=[FIELD_WIDTH + 1, FIELD_WIDTH - 15]))
for ax, plays_, team, col in ((axes[0], PHI, "Eagles", style.OFFENSE_DARK), (axes[1], KC, "Chiefs", style.DEFENSE_DARK)):
    n = len(plays_)
    margin = 4.5 if team == "Eagles" else 13.0
    fld = Field(ax=ax, orient="horizontal", window=None, los=60, to_go=None,
                lateral=None if team == "Eagles" else (8.0, FIELD_WIDTH - 8.0))
    field_extras(fld, pylons=False, border=False)
    for t in ax.texts:
        t.set_alpha(0.25)
    top = FIELD_WIDTH - margin
    gap = (top - margin) / max(1, n - 1)
    for i, play in enumerate(plays_):
        when, what, kind, yl, score = play[:5]
        y = top - i * gap
        if kind == "fg":
            x0 = 120 - yl                                  # the hold: kick distance is measured to the posts
            ax.plot([x0, 119.4], [y, y], color=style.THIRD, lw=1.6, ls=(0, (3, 2)), zorder=5)
            ax.plot([120, 120], [y - 1.4, y + 1.4], color=GOLD, lw=2.4, zorder=6)
            football(ax, x0, y, w=2.2, h=1.3)
        else:
            x0 = 110 - yl
            c = style.THIRD if kind == "ret" else col
            ax.plot([x0, 113.5], [y, y], color=c, lw=2.2, zorder=5, solid_capstyle="round")
            arrow(ax, (112.0, y), (115.5, y), color=c, lw=2.2, head=10)
            if kind == "ret":
                draw_marker(ax, x0, y, "def", "", 6, r=1.3)
            else:
                football(ax, x0, y, w=2.2, h=1.3)
        ax.text(x0 - 2.0, y, f"{when}  {what}", fontsize=6.4, ha="right", va="center", color=style.INK, zorder=8,
                bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.12", fc=style.SURFACE, ec="none", alpha=0.85))
        extra = f"  ({play[5]})" if len(play) > 5 else ""
        ax.text(123.0, y, score + extra, fontsize=6.6, ha="left", va="center", color=style.INK,
                fontweight="bold" if i == n - 1 else "normal")
    ax.text(0, 1.015, f"{team}' scoring plays, attacking left to right", transform=ax.transAxes, fontsize=8.5,
            fontweight="bold", color=col, ha="left", va="bottom")
    ax.set_xlim(-1, 152)
    blank(ax)
fig.subplots_adjust(hspace=0.1, left=0.01, right=0.99, top=0.95, bottom=0.01)
plt.show()
```

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Eagles 2024 — Super Bowl LIX, every score"}
Read the Eagles' panel from the top and you get a tour of this chapter.

- **The goal line is in.** The first touchdown came from a yard out, Jalen Hurts pushed forward
  by his own teammates in the Eagles' famous short-yardage play, the
  [tush push](../10-situational-football/10-03-red-zone-goal-line-and-short-yardage.qmd). One
  yard is all it took because the ball only had to touch the plane.
- **Defenses score too.** Cooper DeJean intercepted Patrick Mahomes at the Kansas City 38 and
  ran it back for a touchdown: six points for the Eagles while their offense sat on the bench.
- **Seven and three.** Philadelphia's scoring was four touchdowns, all followed by Jake Elliott
  extra points (28 points), and four Elliott field goals (12 points): 48, 29, 48 and 50 yards.
  Check the arithmetic on the field: the 50-yarder came from the Chiefs' 32, the 29-yarder from
  their 11, the 48-yarders from their 30. Line of scrimmage plus 18, every time. The 29-yarder
  is the one drive where the Chiefs' defense won the 7-versus-3 battle in the red zone: the
  Eagles reached the 11 and settled for three.
- **Going for two when far behind.** Kansas City scored three touchdowns, all after the game
  was decided, and went for two after every one (one failed, two succeeded): 6 + 8 + 8 = 22.
  When you trail by four scores, one extra point barely matters, and two might cut the number
  of scores you need.
- **The clock.** It was 24–0 at halftime, which is a hard reset: Kansas City got the
  second-half kickoff and new timeouts, but no amount of clock management fixes a 24-point
  hole when an average possession is worth about two points.

What to notice when you watch it again: where each drive *stalled*. The Eagles' field goals
mark the drives the Chiefs' defense held to three; the gap between those four kicks and four
more touchdowns would have been 16 points.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Watch for it on Sunday: the clock watcher"}
Pick one quarter (the second or fourth is best, because of the two-minute warning). Before
**every snap**, say out loud whether the game clock is running, and why.

- **Running?** Look at the score bug before the snap. If it's ticking, the last play ended
  with a tackle in bounds. Say "tackled in bounds."
- **Stopped?** Name the reason: incompletion, out of bounds, timeout, flag, score, change of
  possession, two-minute warning.
- **Out of bounds early in the half?** Watch the clock start again on the referee's signal,
  *before* the snap. Then watch it stay stopped until the snap after the two-minute warning.
- **Count the timeouts** shown in the score bug for each team, and notice when announcers start
  talking about them.
- **Bonus: the hash.** On each snap, note whether the ball is on the left hash, the right hash
  or the middle, and whether the play went to the wide side or the short side.

By the end of one quarter you won't need the chart above. You'll *feel* when the clock should
be running.
:::

## Predict the play

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play 1: which side is the wide side?"}
```{python}
#| label: fig-predict-hash
#| fig-cap: "First-and-10 at the offense's own 40. The ball is on the right hash. The offense lines up three receivers to its left and leaves one (X) alone on the right."
p = Play(offense("gun_trips", strength="left"), None, los=50, ball_y="right", to_go=10)
p.draw(window=(-7.5, 12), lateral="full", title=False)
plt.show()
```

**Which side of this formation is the field side? Why would the offense put its three
receivers there, and what does it give up?**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**The left side is the field (wide) side.** The ball is on the right hash, so there's about 30
yards between the ball and the left sideline and about 24 to the right sideline. The offense put
its three receivers into the bigger space so they have room to spread out and run routes that
break away from each other, and so a run or screen to that side has room to get outside. The
single receiver goes into the boundary, where he works one-on-one against his defender, with the
sideline close by.

What it gives up: three receivers to the field tells the defense where most of the offense's
options are. Defenses that play "field" and "boundary" roles can slide their safeties toward
the wide side and leave the boundary corner alone against X. That is exactly the one-on-one some
offenses *want*, if X is their best receiver. You'll see both versions every Sunday:
"formation to the field" is the common default, and lining up into the boundary is a deliberate
surprise. ([Spread and Modern Formations](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-04-spread-and-modern-formations.qmd)
names this formation; for now, just find the wide side.)
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play 2: out of bounds, or not?"}
```{python}
#| label: fig-predict-clock
#| fig-cap: "Fourth quarter, 3:12 left, the offense trailing 20–24 with no timeouts. Z (outlined) catches a quick out at the sideline 9 yards downfield and steps out of bounds, a yard short of the line to gain."
q = Play(offense("gun_2x2"), defense("nickel", "two_high", offense("gun_2x2")), los=70, to_go=10)
q.dropback(1.0)
q.route("Z", r.out(9, 6.5))
q.pass_to("Z", t=1.9)
q.run("Z", [(0.5, 4.9)])
q.highlight("Z")
fld = q.draw(window=(-7.5, 17), lateral="full", title=False)
fld.ax.text(0.015, 0.97, "Q4  3:12\nTrailing 20–24\nNo timeouts left", transform=fld.ax.transAxes, fontsize=8,
            va="top", ha="left", color=style.INK, fontweight="bold", zorder=20,
            bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.35", fc=style.SURFACE, ec=style.INK_2, lw=0.8))
plt.show()
```

**The clock stopped when Z stepped out. When will it start again? Would your answer change if
this had happened with 6:12 left instead of 3:12?**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**At 3:12 it stays stopped until the next snap.** Inside the last five minutes of the game, a
play that ends out of bounds stops the clock until the ball is snapped again. The offense, with
no timeouts, gets a "free" stoppage just by getting its receiver out, which is exactly why it
threw to the sideline. It can now take its time choosing a play for second-and-1 without
burning clock.

**At 6:12 the answer changes.** Earlier in the half, the clock stops only until the officials
have re-spotted the ball on the hash and the referee signals ready for play. Then it starts
again, and the play clock is running too, so the offense loses most of the advantage.

Now think like the defense, which is protecting a 4-point lead. It wants the clock running, so
it would much rather tackle Z in bounds, even after a few more yards, than let him get out. You'll
see defensive backs play inside their receivers in this situation, taking away the throws over
the middle (where a tackle keeps the clock running anyway) and daring the offense to complete
passes outside before it runs out of time. The detail of the out-of-bounds rule is in
[Clock and Game Management](../10-situational-football/10-04-clock-and-game-management.qmd).
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play 3: three points or seven?"}
```{python}
#| label: fig-predict-goalline
#| fig-cap: "Fourth-and-goal at the 1, second quarter, score tied 7–7. The offense has sent out its heavy goal-line group: three tight ends, a fullback and a tailback. The defense has packed the line. The yellow line to gain is the goal line itself. The kicker is warming up on the sideline."
gl = [q.moved(label="H") if q.key == "W" else q for q in offense("goal_line")]
g = Play(gl, defense("46", "zero", gl), los=109, to_go=1)
fld = g.draw(window=(-9, 11), lateral=(-14, 14), title=False)
field_extras(fld, border=False)
plt.show()
```

**Kick the field goal or go for the touchdown? Put a number on each choice.**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**Go for it, and most NFL coaches now would.** Do it in points:

- **The field goal** is a 19-yarder (the 1 plus 18). From there kickers almost never miss: in
  the 2016–2025 regular seasons, 99% of field goals tried on fourth-and-goal from the 1 or 2
  were good. Call it **3 points**.
- **Going for it** from the 1 or 2 scored a touchdown 55% of the time in the same seasons.
  A touchdown plus an extra point (about 96% good) is worth almost 7, so on average going for
  it is worth about 0.55 × 6.96 ≈ **3.8 points**.[^goalline]

Going for it wins on raw points, and that's before counting the miss. If the offense fails,
the opponent takes over at its own 1-yard line, the worst field position in football. NFL teams
starting a drive there have been, on average, slightly more likely to give up the next score
than to get it. If the kick succeeds, the opponent gets a kickoff and usually starts around its
own 30–35, a much better spot. So even the failure case isn't a disaster, and the success case
is worth four extra points.

That's why teams have changed their behavior: on fourth-and-goal from the 1 or 2, NFL teams
went for it 57% of the time in 2016 and 85% of the time in 2025. The crowd at the top of the
chapter wasn't being irrational when it booed the kicker. It was doing the 7-versus-3 math. How
teams turn this into a fourth-down model, and when the answer flips (late in a game, the score
matters more than the average), is in
[Win Probability and Decision Analysis](../13-analytics-and-data/13-03-win-probability-and-fourth-down.qmd).
:::
:::

## Takeaways

- The field is a 120-yard grid: a 100-yard field of play and two 10-yard end zones. **The goal
  line is in** the end zone, and only the ball has to break its plane; **the sidelines and end
  lines are out**, and any part of the player touching them is enough.
- **Every play starts on or between the hash marks.** With the ball on a hash, the field splits
  into a wide (field) side and a short (boundary) side, and offenses and defenses plan by them. The
  NFL's hashes are narrow, so its field is nearly symmetrical; college's wider hashes make the
  wide side huge.
- Points come in a handful of sizes: **6** for a touchdown, then **1** (kick from the 15) or
  **2** (play from the 2) on the try, **3** for a field goal, and **2 plus the ball** for a
  safety. The **four-point gap between 7 and 3** drives red-zone play, fourth-down decisions and
  late-game math.
- Possessions are scarce, about eleven per team per game, and a team only gets the ball back
  by stopping the other one or after it scores.
- The **game clock** keeps running after a tackle in bounds and stops for incompletions,
  out-of-bounds plays, scores, changes of possession, timeouts and flags; out of bounds stops it
  until the snap only late in each half. The **play clock** gives the offense 40 seconds (or 25)
  to snap. Trailing teams fight to stop the game clock; leading teams make the two clocks run
  together.
- A game is four 15-minute quarters with a two-minute warning near the end of each half, a
  halftime that resets possession and timeouts, and an overtime in which, since 2025, both teams
  get the ball in every game.

[Win Probability and Decision Analysis](../13-analytics-and-data/13-03-win-probability-and-fourth-down.qmd).

**Case studies:** the 2024 Eagles' goal-line game and the tush push appear again in
[Red Zone, Goal Line, and Short Yardage](../10-situational-football/10-03-red-zone-goal-line-and-short-yardage.qmd);
Andy Reid's Chiefs, on both ends of this chapter's film rooms, are the subject of
[Andy Reid's Chiefs](../12-case-studies/12-04-reid-chiefs.qmd).

::: {.callout-note title="Go deeper"}
- The **NFL rulebook** is shorter and more readable than its reputation. Rule 1 (the field),
  Rule 4 (game timing) and Rule 11 (scoring) cover everything in this chapter, at
  operations.nfl.com.
- NFL Football Operations' **"Learn the game"** pages and its glossary of football terms are
  a good plain-English companion.
- Pat Kirwan, *Take Your Eye Off the Ball* (2010; 2nd ed. 2015): written by a former NFL coach
  and scout for fans; good on how the field's landmarks shape what players do.
- The Pro Football Hall of Fame's year-by-year **history pages** trace how hash marks, goal
  posts and scoring rules got where they are.
:::

[^wsj]: David Biderman, "11 Minutes of Action," *The Wall Street Journal* (Jan. 15, 2010), which timed four broadcasts from one late-December weekend and found an average of about 11 minutes of live play (10 minutes 43 seconds) in broadcasts of about three hours (174 minutes): https://www.wsj.com/articles/SB10001424052748704281204575002852055561406 (paywalled; the same study is summarized in a Fox Sports repost, "Football games have 11 minutes of action," Jan. 18, 2010: https://www.foxsports.com/stories/nfl/football-games-have-11-minutes-of-action).

[^field]: NFL, *Official Playing Rules of the National Football League* (2026 edition), Rule 1, Sections 1–2 (a field 360 by 160 feet; end lines, sidelines and goal lines; the 6-foot white border; yard-line markings every 5 yards; inbounds lines "70 feet, 9 inches" from each sideline; 1-yard marks; field numerals whose bottoms begin 12 yards in from each sideline and that are 2 yards tall; the 1-yard-long marks two yards from each goal line), and Rule 3, Section 11, Article 9 (yard lines are named "A's 19," "B's 49"): https://operations.nfl.com/the-rules/nfl-rulebook/

[^plane]: NFL rulebook (2026), Rule 11, Section 2, Article 1 (a touchdown when the ball is "on, above, or behind the plane of the opponent's goal line," including a ball that passes "over or inside the pylon"); Rule 3, Section 11, Article 3 ("The goal line and the pylons are in the end zone"); Rule 3, Section 20, Article 1 (a player is out of bounds "when he touches a boundary line"): https://operations.nfl.com/the-rules/nfl-rulebook/

[^posts]: NFL rulebook (2026), Rule 1, Section 3: a crossbar 18 feet 6 inches long whose top is 10 feet above the ground, "in the plane of each end line," and uprights that "extend 35 feet above the crossbar": https://operations.nfl.com/the-rules/nfl-rulebook/

[^firstplayoff]: Pro Football Hall of Fame, "The First Playoff Game": the December 18, 1932 Bears–Spartans game was moved into Chicago Stadium on a field "only 80 yards long and 30 feet narrower" than regulation, with "the sidelines butted up against the stands"; for 1933 the league required "the ball be spotted on the hashmarks on every play" and moved the goal posts "from the end line to the goal line": https://profootballhof.com/football-history/the-first-playoff-game . Accounts of the game's special sideline rule differ (some say the ball went to inbounds lines 10 yards from the walls, others that it could be brought in 15 yards at the cost of a down): "1932 NFL Playoff Game," Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1932_NFL_Playoff_Game . Before 1933, "all plays began where the ball was declared dead": "Hash mark (sports)," Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hash_marks

[^hash72]: Pro Football Hall of Fame, NFL history by year: 1933 ("inbounds line or hashmarks ... adopted" from the 1932 game), https://www.profootballhof.com/football-history/football-history/1869-1939/1933 ; 1935 ("moved nearer the center of the field, 15 yards from the sidelines"), https://www.profootballhof.com/football-history/football-history/1869-1939/1935 ; 1945 ("moved from 15 yards away from the sidelines to nearer the center of the field - 20 yards from the sidelines"), https://www.profootballhof.com/football-history/football-history/1940-1959/1945 ; 1972 ("moved nearer the center of the field, 23 yards, 1 foot, 9 inches from the sidelines"), https://www.profootballhof.com/football-history/football-history/1960-1979/1972 . The 1933 distance (10 yards, i.e. 30 feet) is from "Hash mark (sports)," Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hash_marks

[^offense72]: The motive: the Associated Press report of the owners' vote ran as "Owners give offense big seven-yard boost" (*Rome News-Tribune*, Mar. 24, 1972, p. 6A, cited in "1972 NFL season," Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1972_NFL_season); *Sports Illustrated*, "High on the Hash" (Aug. 28, 1972), tied it to the low scoring of 1971: https://vault.si.com/vault/1972/08/28/high-on-the-hash

[^collegehash]: NFL Football Operations, 2026 rulebook page, field markings: "The location of the inbounds hash marks is 70' 9" for professional football, 60' for college football": https://operations.nfl.com/the-rules/nfl-rulebook/ (the NCAA rules, Rule 1-2, likewise put the inbounds lines 60 feet from the sidelines). College hashes have been 40 feet apart since 1993, the spacing the NFL used from 1945 to 1971, and high-school hashes are 53 feet 4 inches from each sideline: "Hash mark (sports)," Wikipedia, citing the *Milwaukee Journal* (Mar. 26, 1993): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hash_marks

[^scorevalues]: NFL rulebook (2026), Rule 11, Section 1, Article 2 (touchdown 6, field goal 3, safety 2, try 1 or 2); Rule 11, Section 3 (the try: snapped "15 yards from the defensive team's goal line for a Try kick" or "two yards" for a run or pass; the game clock does not run; two points for a touchdown by either team; one point for what would ordinarily be a safety): https://operations.nfl.com/the-rules/nfl-rulebook/

[^xp2015]: NFL.com, "NFL moves extra point to 15-yard line for 2015 season" (May 2015), which also reports the new rule letting the defense return a blocked kick or failed two-point try for two points: https://www.nfl.com/news/nfl-moves-extra-point-to-15-yard-line-for-2015-season-0ap3000000493347

[^twopt]: Pro Football Hall of Fame, "2-point conversion turns 30 years old" (2024): https://www.profootballhof.com/news/2-point-conversion-turns-30-years-old ; *Deseret News*, "NFL officially adopts 2-point conversion" (Mar. 23, 1994): https://www.deseret.com/1994/3/23/19098606/nfl-officially-adopts-2-point-conversion/ . College football has used it since 1958 and the AFL used it from 1960 to 1969 (same PFHOF article).

[^trycalc]: Course calculation from nflverse play-by-play, regular seasons 2010–2025: rows with an `extra_point_result` (kicks) or a `two_point_conv_result` (two-point tries), success = "good" or "success". Tries nullified by penalties are not counted.

[^fgcalc]: Course calculation from nflverse play-by-play, regular seasons: all field-goal attempts by `kick_distance`, 2021–2025 for the chart; 2025 alone for the count of made kicks of 60+ yards. Kicks of 50+ yards were made 57% of the time in 2016 and 58% in 2019, against 69–70% in every season from 2022 to 2025.

[^goalposts74]: Pro Football Hall of Fame, NFL history by year, 1974 ("the goal posts were moved from the goal line to the end lines," part of a package of changes adopted "to add action and tempo to games"): https://www.profootballhof.com/football-history/football-history/1960-1979/1974 . On the purpose, Nexstar Media, "NFL goalposts used to look very different: What changed, and why they moved" (2025), citing the Hall of Fame: the move was made "in an effort to force offenses to play for touchdowns instead of field goals," and attempts fell from more than 860 the season before to 553: https://www.abc27.com/news/nfl-goalposts-used-to-look-very-different-what-changed-and-why-they-moved/

[^safety]: NFL rulebook (2026), Rule 11, Section 5 (what is a safety; after a safety, "the team scored upon must put the ball in play by a free kick (punt, drop kick, or place kick) from its 20-yard line"): https://operations.nfl.com/the-rules/nfl-rulebook/ . The count is a course calculation from nflverse play-by-play (`safety == 1`), 2025 regular season, 272 games.

[^drives]: Course calculation from nflverse play-by-play, 2025 regular season (272 games): one row per drive (`fixed_drive`), classified by `fixed_drive_result`; a red-zone trip is a drive with `drive_inside20 == 1`; points per team are final scores averaged over both teams.

[^timing]: NFL rulebook (2026), Rule 4, Section 1 (four 15-minute periods; at least two minutes between the first and second and the third and fourth periods; a 13-minute halftime) and Section 2 (the visiting captain calls the coin toss; the winner may defer; teams change goals after the first and third periods with possession, down, ball position and line to gain unchanged): https://operations.nfl.com/the-rules/nfl-rulebook/

[^defer]: The option to defer was added in 2008. Coin-toss winners deferred 8% of the time in 2008 and 76% in the first half of the 2015 season (Ben Goessling, ESPN, Nov. 5, 2015, "For NFL teams, deferring after winning coin toss is more than a 50-50 choice": https://www.espn.com/blog/nfcnorth/post/_/id/72630/for-nfl-teams-deferring-after-winning-coin-toss-is-more-than-a-50-50-choice) and about five times in six by 2018 (Zach Barnett, FootballScoop, "The number of NFL coaches deferring the kickoff has skyrocketed in the past decade," Sept. 7, 2018: https://footballscoop.com/news/number-nfl-coaches-deferring-kickoff-skyrocketed-past-decade).

[^kickoff]: NFL.com, "NFL owners vote to make dynamic kickoff permanent, adjust ball spot on touchbacks to 35-yard line" (2025): https://www.nfl.com/news/nfl-owners-vote-to-make-dynamic-kickoff-permanent-adjust-ball-spot-on-touchbacks-to-35-yard-line ; Seattle Seahawks, "NFL announces approved rule changes for 2026 season" (onside kick declarable at any time): https://www.seahawks.com/news/nfl-announces-approved-rule-changes-for-2026-season . The kicker's restraining line is the kicking team's 35 (2026 rulebook, Rule 6, Section 1, Article 2).

[^twomin]: NFL rulebook (2026), Rule 3, Section 41: "an automatic timeout that occurs at the conclusion of the last down for which the ball is legally snapped or kicked prior to two minutes remaining on the game clock in the second and fourth periods." On its origin: Football Zebras, "NFL100: For half of NFL history, the official time was not on the scoreboard" (Oct. 2019), which notes that official time moved to the scoreboard when the NFL adopted the AFL's rule at the 1970 merger and that "the two-minute warning was just that — an official notification to both sidelines": https://www.footballzebras.com/2019/10/nfl100-for-half-of-nfl-history-the-official-time-was-not-on-the-scoreboard

[^ot]: NFL Football Operations, "Featured rules" (overtime: playoffs since 2022 and regular season since 2025, both teams possess; regular-season period of 10 minutes, ties possible): https://operations.nfl.com/rules-officiating/featured-rules ; ESPN, NFL rule changes for 2025: https://www.espn.com/nfl/story/_/id/46088927/nfl-rules-changes-tush-push-chain-gang-kickoffs-celebrations . Timeouts in overtime: 2026 rulebook, Rule 4, Section 5, Article 1.

[^plays]: Course calculation from nflverse play-by-play, 2025 regular season: runs, passes, punts, field goals, extra points, kickoffs, kneels and spikes per game, both teams together (about 149), of which runs and passes about 121.

[^clockrules]: NFL rulebook (2026), Rule 4, Section 3 (starting the game clock: after a free kick "when the ball is legally touched in the field of play"; after a runner goes out of bounds, "on the Referee's signal that a ball has been returned to play," except on the snap after a change of possession, after the two-minute warning of the first half, or inside the last five minutes of the second half; after fouls, generally "as if the foul had not occurred," with late-game exceptions) and Section 4 (stopping the game clock): https://operations.nfl.com/the-rules/nfl-rulebook/

[^ncaa]: ESPN, "NCAA approves rule change to run clock after first downs" (Apr. 21, 2023; the change applies in every division except Division III, and the clock still stops after first downs in the last two minutes of each half): https://www.espn.com/college-football/story/_/id/36255797/ncaa-approves-rule-change-run-clock-first-downs

[^timeouts]: NFL rulebook (2026), Rule 4, Section 5, Article 1: "three charged team timeouts during each half and two timeouts during an overtime period in the regular season"; a second timeout by the defense to "freeze" a kicker is unsportsmanlike conduct (Item 4): https://operations.nfl.com/the-rules/nfl-rulebook/

[^playclock]: NFL rulebook (2026), Rule 4, Section 6, Articles 1–2: "within 40 seconds after the start of the play clock," which starts "when a play ends"; 25 seconds "beginning with the Referee's whistle" after administrative stoppages including a change of possession, a charged team timeout, the two-minute warning, the expiration of a period and a penalty enforcement: https://operations.nfl.com/the-rules/nfl-rulebook/

[^thirteen]: Play sequence, times and scores from nflverse play-by-play, game `2021_20_BUF_KC` (Jan. 23, 2022), including the touchbacks, the timeouts at 0:08 and 0:03, Harrison Butker's 49-yard field goal and the overtime touchdown; the overtime rule changes as in the NFL Football Operations "Featured rules" page and this course's fact sheet (checked 2026-10-06).

[^lix]: Date, venue, score and MVP (Jalen Hurts) as in this course's fact sheet (checked 2026-10-06), e.g. CBS News, "Jalen Hurts named Super Bowl MVP": https://www.cbsnews.com/amp/news/nfl-mvp-super-bowl-jalen-hurts-eagles . Every scoring play, its time, spot and kick distance from nflverse play-by-play, game `2024_22_KC_PHI`.

[^goalline]: Course calculation from nflverse play-by-play, 2016–2025 regular seasons: fourth-and-goal snaps from the 1 or 2 (593 plays): runs and passes scored a touchdown on 55% (236 of 426); field goals were good on 99% (166 of 167); teams went for it on 57% of these snaps in 2016 and 85% in 2025. Expected points for a first-and-10 at a team's own 1-yard line averaged about −0.5 in 2023–2025 (nflverse `ep`), against about +1.6 at its own 35.
